Exec dinners for everyone. Or webinars for everyone. Or customer panels for everyone.

2️⃣ Anecdotal feedback from internal attendees.

What conversations happened? What did we learn? What feedback did we get?
This isn't Salesforce data. It's qualitative. But it matters.

3️⃣ One month, three months later...what happened to those deals?

Zach looks back at who attended the dinner and tracks what happened to their opportunities.

They're trying to improve Salesforce reporting. But the honest answer? For Supper Club specifically, it's really difficult to create an attribution machine.

Why?

Because it's so high-touch and so low-volume.

You can't measure a 15-person dinner the way you measure a webinar with 500 registrants. The data isn't there. The volume isn't there.

Most marketers try to force attribution anyway.

They create custom campaign tags. They build complex multi-touch models. 

They try to "prove" the dinner influenced the deal.

But high-touch events don't fit into attribution models cleanly. There's too much happening offline. Too many conversations that don't log in Salesforce.

Zach's approach: measure what actually matters.

Did the prospect engage deeply enough that they'd have paid for the dinner themselves? That's signal.

Did internal attendees report meaningful conversations? That's signal.

Did deals close or accelerate in the months after? That's signal.

None of that fits neatly into a Salesforce report. But it's real.

The trap most marketers fall into is that they kill high-touch, low-volume programs because they can't prove attribution in a dashboard.

But some of the highest-ROI marketing activities are impossible to attribute cleanly. Executive dinners. Boardroom briefings. Deep customer workshops.

If you only run programs you can measure in Salesforce, you're leaving the highest-leverage work on the table.

Zach's measuring what matters: behavior change.

If a prospect goes from "delayed conversations" to "introducing you to my direct reports to get the POC off the ground," that's success.

Even if Salesforce can't track it.

You don't get creative sitting in status update meetings or obsessing over Gantt charts.

The team becomes order-takers.

They're executing the process. They're checking boxes. They're following the playbook.

But they're not thinking creatively. They're not taking risks. They're not coming up with the ideas that actually move the business.

Marcy's point is that process is important. But it's not the CMO's job to fixate on it.

Someone process-oriented should own it. A marketing ops person. A chief of staff. A project manager.

But the CMO? The CMO's job is to create the conditions for creativity to happen.

So if you're a CMO and you're spending most of your time in project management tools and status meetings, ask:

Am I creating the conditions for creativity? Or am I killing it with process?
